'''''Xanthosoma sagittifolium''''', or '''tannia''', is a tropical flowering plant from the family [[Araceae]]. It produces an edible, starchy [[corm]]. ''X. sagittifolium'' is native to tropical America where it has been first cultivated. Around the 19th century, the plant spread to Southeast Asia and Africa and has been cultivated there ever since. ''X. sagittifolium'' is often confused with the related plant ''Colocasia esculenta'' ([[taro]]), which is similar both in appearance and its uses. Both plants are often collectively named '[[cocoyam]]'.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Onwueme |first1=I. C. |title=Tropical root and tuber crops: production, perspectives and future prospects |last2=Charles |first2=W. B. |date=1994 |publisher=FAO |others=FAO |isbn=978-92-5-103461-3 |series=FAO plant production and protection paper |location=Rome}}</ref>

Tannia is among the world’s most important tuber crops and feeds 400 million people worldwide.<ref name="Utilizing cocoyam (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) for food and nutrition security: A review">{{Cite journal |last1=Boakye |first1=Abena A. |last2=Wireko-Manu |first2=Faustina Dufie |last3=Oduro |first3=Ibok |last4=Ellis |first4=William O. |last5=Gudjónsdóttir |first5=María |last6=Chronakis |first6=Ioannis S. |date=June 2018 |title=Utilizing cocoyam (''Xanthosoma sagittifolium'') for food and nutrition security: A review |journal=Food Science & Nutrition |language=en |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=703–713 |doi=10.1002/fsn3.602 |doi-access=free |issn=2048-7177 |pmc=6021709 |pmid=29983932}}</ref> There are multiple varieties,<ref name="Agronomic characteristics (varieties or landraces) and potential of Xanthosoma sagittifolium as food and starch source">{{Citation |last1=Siqueira |first1=Marcos Vinicius Bohrer Monteiro |chapter=Chapter 13 - Agronomic characteristics (varieties or landraces) and potential of Xanthosoma sagittifolium as food and starch source |date=2023-01-01 |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780323900577000103 |title=Varieties and Landraces: Cultural Practices and Traditional Uses |volume=2 |pages=261–272 |editor-last=Pascoli Cereda |editor-first=Marney |access-date=2023-11-29 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-323-90057-7 |last2=do Nascimento |first2=Wellington Ferreira |last3=Pedrosa |first3=Marinalva Woods |last4=Veasey |first4=Elizabeth Ann |editor2-last=François Vilpoux |editor2-first=Olivier}}</ref> the two most common being the red flesh and the white flesh variety.<ref name="Starch structure and some properties of cocoyam (Xanthosoma sagittifolium and Colocasia esculenta) starch and raphides">{{Cite journal |last1=Sefa-Dedeh |first1=Samuel |last2=Kofi-Agyir Sackey |first2=Emmanuel |date=2002-12-01 |title=Starch structure and some properties of cocoyam (Xanthosoma sagittifolium and Colocasia esculenta) starch and raphides |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0308814602001942 |journal=Food Chemistry |volume=79 |issue=4 |pages=435–444 |doi=10.1016/S0308-8146(02)00194-2 |issn=0308-8146|url-access=subscription }}</ref> They were [[Selective breeding|selectively bred]] to improve pest and disease resistance,<ref name="Edible Aroids">{{Citation |last1=O'Hair |first1=S. == Common names ==

K. |title=Edible Medicinal and non Medicinal Plants |year=2015 |isbn=978-94-017-9510-4 |pages=498–509 |chapter=Xanthosoma sagittifolium |doi=10.1007/978-94-017-9511-1_15}}</ref><ref name=":3" /> and '''{{lang|es|uncucha}}'''.<ref>{{cite book |author1=Nigel Maxted |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CJxrCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA307 |title=Plant Genetic Conservation: The in situ approach |author2=B.V. Ford-Lloyd |author3=J.G. Hawkes |date=2013 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=9789400914377 |page=309 |access-date=3 October 2024}}</ref> Cultivars with purple stems or leaves are also variously called blue taro, purplestem taro, purplestem tannia, and purple elephant's ear.<ref name="tb">{{cite web |title=''Xanthosoma violaceum'' |url=http://www.tropicalbritain.co.uk/aroids/xanthosoma/xanthosoma-violaceum/xanthosoma-violaceum.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202085443/http://www.tropicalbritain.co.uk/aroids/xanthosoma/xanthosoma-violaceum/xanthosoma-violaceum.html |archive-date=2 February 2017 |access-date=22 January 2017 |publisher=Tropical Britain}}</ref><ref name="tb2">{{cite web |title=Xanthosoma violaceum from Tropical Britain - Purple Elephant's Ears |url=https://www.tropicalbritain.co.uk/xanthosoma-saggittifolium.html |access-date=10 May 2022 |publisher=Tropical Britain}}</ref>

== Ecology ==

=== Diseases ===
[[Root rot]] is the most important disease in tannia. The oomycete ''[[Pythium myriotylum]]'' is probably the main causal agent of the root rot disease. Other organisms that could be involved are ''[[Phytophthora|Phytopthora]]'' ssp., ''[[Fusarium]]'' ssp., ''[[Penicillium]]'' ssp., ''Botrydioplodia'' ssp., ''[[Erwinia]]'' ssp. and ''[[Pseudomonas]]'' ssp.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pacumbaba |first1=R. P. |last2=Wutoh |first2=J. G. |last3=Eyango |first3=Sama Anne |last4=Tambong |first4=J. T. |last5=Nyochembeng |first5=L. M. |date=1992 |title=Isolation and Pathogenicity of Rhizosphere Fungi of Cocoyam in Relation to Cocoyam Root Rot Disease |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1439-0434.1992.tb04312.x |journal=Journal of Phytopathology |language=en |volume=135 |issue=4 |pages=265–273 |doi=10.1111/j.1439-0434.1992.tb04312.x |issn=0931-1785 |url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Reddy |first=P. Parvatha |title=Plant protection in tropical root and tuber crops |date=2015 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-81-322-2388-7 |location=New Delhi Heidelberg New York, NY Dordrecht London}}{{page needed|date=January 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Breeding of Neglected and Under-Utilized Crops, Spices, and Herbs |date=2007-01-06 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=9780429083297 |editor-last=Ochatt |editor-first=Sergio |edition=First |pages=269–316 |chapter=Genetic Improvement and Utilization of Major Under-utilized Crops in India |doi=10.1201/9781482280548-22}}</ref> Symptoms are stunted growth, wilting, chlorotic and withered leaves and a poor root system. The disease leads to low yields or even complete crop failure.<ref name=":5">{{Cite conference |last1=Wutoh |first1=J.G. |last2=Tambong |first2=J.T. |last3=Meboka |first3=M.M. |last4=Nzietchueng |first4=S. |date=1994 |title=Field Evaluation of Cocoyam (''Xanthosoma Sagittifolium'' (L) SCHOTT) For Tolerance to the Root Rot Disease caused by ''Pythium Myriotylum'' |conference=Symposium on Tropical Root Crops in a Developing Economy |location=Accra, Ghana |issue=380 |pages=462–466 |doi=10.17660/actahortic.1994.380.71 |issn=0567-7572 |journal=Acta Horticulturae |editor-last1=Ofori |editor-first1=F. |editor-last2=Hahn |editor-first2=S.K.}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Onyeka |first=Joseph |date=2014 |title=Status of Cocoyam (''Colocasia esculenta'' and ''Xanthosoma spp'') in West and Central Africa: Production, Household Importance and the Threat from Leaf Blight |url=https://cgspace.cgiar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/6675eefa-76f5-44a3-8b33-72b0a289e62e/content |access-date=30 January 2025 |publisher=CGIAR Research Program on Roots, Tubers and Bananas (RTB) |location=Lima, Peru}}</ref> The disease spreads through soil and planting material. The pathogens can persist for a long time in the soil, often forcing farmers to give up planting tannia in infected fields for at least five years. Wetland, floodings and poorly drained soils are associated with the appearance of root rot disease. As long as the field is not yet infected, the best method to control the disease is to use disease-free planting material. Further cultural control methods are general strengthening of plant health, drainage, crop rotation and planting on ridges. There are cultivars that are less susceptible to root rot, but none of them are resistant. Various fungicides are effective in case of infection.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" />

[[Dasheen Mosaic Potyvirus]] is the most important virus that infects tannia and other aroids. Symptoms include chlorotic mosaic patterns along the veins and stunting. The Dasheen Mosaic Virus is not lethal but can reduce the yield significantly. The virus is transmitted by aphids. It can be spread vegetatively by planting material and mechanically by sap transmission while using tools. It is therefore important to use virus-free plant material and to work hygienically. The control of the vector aphids would be effective, but is difficult.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=REYES |first1=G. |last2=RÖNNBERG-WÄSTLJUNG |first2=A. C. |last3=NYMAN |first3=M. |date=2006 |title=COMPARISON OF FIELD PERFORMANCE BETWEEN DASHEEN MOSAIC VIRUS-FREE AND VIRUS-INFECTED ''IN VITRO'' PLANTS OF COCOYAM ( ''XANTHOSOMA'' spp.) IN NICARAGUA |journal=Experimental Agriculture |volume=42 |issue=3 |pages=301–310 |doi=10.1017/s0014479706003590 |issn=0014-4797 |s2cid=85098812}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Nelson |first=Scot C. |date=August 2008 |title=Dasheen Mosaic of Edible and Ornamental Aroids |url=http://hdl.handle.net/10125/12392 |series=Plant Disease |publisher=University of Hawaii |language=en-US |id=Cooperative Extension Service Publication No. PD-44 |location=Honolulu |hdl=10125/12392}}</ref>

[[Taro leaf blight]], caused by ''Phytophthora colocasiae'', is not a problem in tannia. Some varieties of tannia even seem to be resistant against it.  By contrast, in [[taro]] (''Colocasia esculenta''), a related and similar-looking crop plant, this is a major disease problem.<ref name=":6" />

== Cultivation ==

=== Climate requirements ===
Although its exact native range is uncertain, the plant is now widely cultivated in the American tropics. This cultivation is not only for ornamental purposes but also, both privately and commercially, for its edible parts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Xanthosoma sagittifolium - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=276540#:~:text=Xanthosoma%20sagittifolium,%20commonly%20called%20tannia,for%20certain%20edible%20plant%20parts. |access-date=2024-05-22 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref> ''Xanthosoma sagittifolium'' is an adaptable plant that grows optimally in warm and humid conditions and temperatures above 25 degrees Celsius.<ref name=":3">Siqueira, M., Nascimento, W., Pedrosa, M., & Veasey, E. (2023). Agronomic characteristics (varieties or landraces) and potential of Xanthosoma sagittifolium as food and starch source. In M. P. Cereda & O. F. Vilpoux (Eds.), Varieties and Landraces (pp. 261–272). Academic Press. https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-323-90057-7.00010-3</ref> At lower temperatures and in arid climates, the development of the plant is hindered. For proper development, the plant needs rainfall evenly distributed throughout the year.<ref name=":1">Jagtap, K. B., & Vilas, C. A. (2017). Tannia. In M. K. Rana (Ed.), Vegetable Crop Science (1st ed.) (pp. 79–86). CRC Press.</ref>

It is noteworthy that tannia is one of the most shade-tolerant plants, which allows successful cultivation in traditional [[Agroforestry]] systems and facilitates [[intercropping]] with [[Perennial plant|perennial]] crops such as bananas, cocoas or oil palms.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">Manner, H. I. (2011). Farm and Forestry Production and Marketing Profile for Tannia. In C. R. Elevitch (Ed.), Speciality Crops for Pacific Island Agroforestry.</ref>

The optimal soil conditions for the plant to thrive are well-drained, [[loam]]y soils with a pH between 5.5 and 6.5.<ref name=":1" /> However, Tannia can grow in various soil types, with the exception of hard clay or pure sand, but generally prefers soils high in organic matter.<ref name=":2" /> In general, the plant's adaptability allows it to flourish in a wide range of soils and habitats.

=== Planting ===
The best time for planting depends on the local climatic conditions of the growing region. However, it is suggested to do the planting during the rainy season and when the soil is sufficiently moist.<ref name=":1" />

Small parts of the [[corm]]s or cormels are used for planting. These propagating materials are typically planted at a depth of 7–10 cm, ideally with the growth bud pointing downward.<ref name=":2" /> Planting is done in rows half a meter to one meter apart to allow the corms and cormels to develop well and to facilitate the harvest.<ref name=":1" /> More dense planting leads to higher yields per field and less weeding, more space results in a higher yield per plant but more weeding work.<ref name=":2" /> Crop Management is done manually using simple tools such as digging sticks or bush knives.

=== Harvesting ===
The typical tannia plant has a 9 to 11 months growing cycle.<ref name=":0">Opara, L. U. (2003). Edible Aroids: Post-Harvest Operation. Massey University, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.</ref> During this time, it produces a large stem called a corm, which is surrounded by smaller edible cormels about the size of potatoes. Harvesting these edible [[Araceae|aroids]] typically occurs when the leaves start to turn yellow. During the growth cycle, a plant typically produces approximately 40-50 leaves, which are usually harvested within a 40-50 day period.<ref name=":1" />

Mature cormels can be harvested continuously over an extended period of time, often exceeding 500 days, while the primary mother plant remains in the ground to produce a new crop.<ref name=":0" />

Harvesting is commonly carried out manually or with semi-mechanized equipment. After harvesting, the corms are cured to slow down the rate of physiological and pathological decay of the tuber, which would result in loss of quality.<ref name=":0" /> Further losses may occur due to the short shelf life of the tubers. Also storage at ambient temperatures poses a challenge.

== Nutrition ==

Tannia is an important source of starch in many African countries such as Ethiopia. Its tubers contain approximately 85% [[carbohydrates]] in dry matter.<ref>Wada, E., Feyissa, T. & Tesfaye, K. (2019). Proximate, mineral and antinutrient contents of Cocoyam (Xanthosoma sagittifolium (L.) Schott) from Ethiopia. International journal of food science, 2019, 1–7. https://doi.org/10.1155/2019/8965476</ref> Furthermore, the [[protein]] content amounts to 10% – a benefit for the resource-poor farmers by whom Tannia is mainly consumed. The plant is also rich in [[vitamin A]] and [[vitamin C]] and a good source of [[potassium]], [[calcium]] and other minerals.<ref>Siqueira, M. V. B. M., Nascimento, W. F. D., Pedrosa, M. W. & Veasey, E. A. (2023). Agronomic characteristics (varieties or landraces) and potential of Xanthosoma sagittifolium as food and starch source. In Elsevier eBooks (S. 261–272). https://doi.org/10.1016/b978-0-323-90057-7.00010-3</ref>

However, the presence of [[calcium oxalate]] must be considered,{{citation needed|date=January 2025}} a compound known to irritate [[mucous membranes]], resulting in crystalline deposits commonly referred to as crystal sand. Consumption of these corms can lead to a scratchy sensation in the mouth and throat. To mitigate this effect, the corms need to be boiled before consumption, as this process allows the substances to dissolve in the cooking water, making the corms safe to eat.{{citation needed|date=January 2025}}

== Uses ==

===Culinary===
{{More citations needed section|date=May 2022}}
Tannia is a versatile crop with both its corm and leaves suitable for human consumption. The corms can be categorized into smaller secondary corms and main corms. Secondary corms are primarily used in various culinary applications, in similar ways as potatoes. They can be boiled, fried, roasted, steamed, baked, or ground into [[flour]]. The leaves of the tannia plant find common culinary use as a leafy green, similar to spinach. In contrast, primary corms are typically designated for animal feed rather than human consumption because of the higher amount of oxalates.<ref name="Edible Aroids" />{{Additional citation needed|date=September 2025}}

In [[Bolivia]], it is called ''walusa'', in [[Colombia]] ''bore'', in [[Costa Rica]] ''tiquizque'' or ''macal'', in [[Cuba]] {{lang|es|malanga}}, in [[Mexico]] {{lang|es|mafafa}}, in [[Nicaragua]] {{lang|es|quequisque}}, in [[Panama]] {{lang|es|otoe}}, in [[Dominican Republic cuisine|Dominican cuisine]] is called {{lang|es|yautía}}, {{lang|es|yautía morada}}, and {{lang|es|yautía coco}} and {{lang|es|ocumo}} in [[Venezuela]]. In [[Brazil]], the leaves are sold as {{lang|pt-BR|taioba}}. The tuber (called {{lang|es|nampi}} or {{lang|es|malanga}}) is also used in the cuisine of these countries. The plant is often interplanted within [[reforestation]] areas to control weeds and provide shade during the early stages of growth.

In [[Cuisine of Puerto Rico|Puerto Rican cuisine]] and [[Dominican Republic cuisine|Dominican cuisine]], the plant and its corm are called {{lang|es|yautía}}. In Dominican Republic as well as in Puerto Rican ''[[pasteles en hoja]]'', {{lang|es|yautía}} is ground with squash, potato, green bananas and plantains into a dough-like fluid paste containing pork and ham, and boiled in a banana leaf or paper wrapper.  The {{lang|es|yautía}} corm is used in stews, soups, or simply served boiled much like a [[potato]]. It is used in local dishes such as ''[[guanime]]'', ''[[alcapurria]]s'', ''[[sancocho]]'', and ''[[mondongo]]''. In ''alcapurrias'', it is also ground with green bananas and made into fried [[croquette]]s containing ''[[picadillo]]'' or seafood. {{lang|es|Yautía majada}} is also prepared and consumed when mashed in some instances. {{lang|es|Yautía}} puree is usually served with fish or shellfish cooked in coconut milk.

In [[Suriname]] and the [[Netherlands]], the plant is called ''tayer''. The shredded root is baked with chicken, fruit juices, salted meat, and spices in the popular Surinamese dish, [[Pom (dish)|''pom'']].  Eaten over rice or on bread, ''pom'' is commonly eaten in Suriname at family gatherings and on special occasions, and is also popular throughout the Netherlands. In Surinamese cuisine the leaves are also often baked with a [[Maggi]]-cube (chicken boullion cube) and eaten alongside rice and chicken or salted beef.

=== Flour ===
Flour can be made by slicing the rhizome and then drying it. Afterwards, it can be finely ground. The yield of the starch is about 15%.<ref name="Production and characterization of tannia rhizome flour">{{Cite journal |last1=Morais |first1=A. F. |last2=Canapá |first2=L. B. S. |last3=Silveira |first3=M. F. A. |last4=Vera |first4=R. |date=2020-09-01 |title=Production and characterization of tannia rhizome flour |url=https://sea.ufr.edu.br/index.php?journal=SEA&page=article&op=view&path[]=1201 |journal=Scientific Electronic Archives |volume=13 |issue=9 |pages=67 |doi=10.36560/13920201201 |issn=2316-9281 |doi-access=free}}</ref>
A big problem of tannia is the low storability because of the high moisture content of the [[corm]]s and cormels.<ref name="Characterization of some properties of starches isolated from Xanthosoma sagittifolium (tannia) and Colocassia esculenta (taro)">{{Cite journal |last1=Pérez |first1=Elevina |last2=Schultz |first2=Forrest S. |last3=de Delahaye |first3=Emperatríz Pacheco |date=2005-05-06 |title=Characterization of some properties of starches isolated from Xanthosoma sagittifolium (tannia) and Colocassia esculenta (taro) |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0144861704004618 |journal=Carbohydrate Polymers |volume=60 |issue=2 |pages=139–145 |doi=10.1016/j.carbpol.2004.11.033 |issn=0144-8617 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> Processing the tubers into flour could increase the storability of the crop and could increase the added value. Local farmers then would be able to sell their crop for a higher price, which could then help the local community.<ref name="Characterization of some properties of starches isolated from Xanthosoma sagittifolium (tannia) and Colocassia esculenta (taro)" /> Especially the white fleshed variety provides flour that has qualities that are great for making bread, since the resulting paste is not as cohesive and can therefore be used for the preparation of different foods.<ref name="Starch structure and some properties of cocoyam (Xanthosoma sagittifolium and Colocasia esculenta) starch and raphides" /> Flour could also easily be used in meat and milk products.<ref name="Production and characterization of tannia rhizome flour" /> A disadvantage of the flour is the (especially in comparison with flour made from cassava) lower starch content and it therefore would be best to only make flour as a byproduct of other processes.<ref name="Utilizing cocoyam (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) for food and nutrition security: A review" /> It could also be made from cormels that do not provide the necessary quality for cooking.<ref name="Yautia (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) in the food culture of Puerto Rico">{{Citation |last1=Chávez Jáuregui |first1=Rosa N. |chapter=Chapter 14 - Yautía (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) in the food culture of Puerto Rico |date=2023-01-01 |title=Varieties and Landraces: Cultural Practices and Traditional Uses |volume=2 |pages=273–287 |editor-last=Pascoli Cereda |editor-first=Marney |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780323900577000152 |access-date=2023-12-01 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-323-90057-7 |last2=Vega |first2=Ángel Bosques |last3=Wessel-Beaver |first3=Linda |editor2-last=François Vilpoux |editor2-first=Olivier}}</ref>

=== Chicken feed ===
Studies have shown that it is possible to replace up to 45% of the [[maize]] grain in chicken feed with tannia corm meal (TCM). This could be useful for farmers since chicken feed which consists of maize grains is very expensive, especially in poorer countries. At the beginning of their growing phase, chickens fed with TCM consume significantly more because TCM reduces the nutrient uptake and weight gain. Later in the growing stage, this effect diminishes and in the end, there is no difference in the weight of chickens fed with TCM in comparison to chickens fed entirely with maize grains.<ref name="Effects of different graded levels of tannia (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) on growth performance of broiler chicken">{{Cite journal |last1=Edmew |first1=Tewabe |last2=Muleta |first2=Eyerus |last3=Worku |first3=Zemene |date=2023-12-31 |title=Effects of different graded levels of tannia ( Xanthosoma sagittifolium ) on growth performance of broiler chicken |journal=Cogent Food & Agriculture |language=en |volume=9 |issue=1 |bibcode=2023CogFA...952553E |doi=10.1080/23311932.2023.2252553 |issn=2331-1932 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Other uses ===
Tannia is used by some populations as a medicine against tarantula, scorpion and snake bites.<ref name="Utilizing cocoyam (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) for food and nutrition security: A review" /> Studies with rats have shown that tannia leaves could protect from [[cardiovascular disease]]s<ref name="Cholesterol reducing and bile-acid binding properties of taioba (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) leaf in rats fed a high-fat diet">{{Cite journal |last1=de Almeida Jackix |first1=Elisa |last2=Monteiro |first2=Elisa Bernardes |last3=Raposo |first3=Helena Fonseca |last4=Amaya-Farfán |first4=Jaime |date=2013-05-01 |title=Cholesterol reducing and bile-acid binding properties of taioba (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) leaf in rats fed a high-fat diet |journal=Food Research International |volume=51 |issue=2 |pages=886–891 |doi=10.1016/j.foodres.2013.02.017 |issn=0963-9969 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and bowel cancer.<ref name="Agronomic characteristics (varieties or landraces) and potential of Xanthosoma sagittifolium as food and starch source" /> Other benefits include a reduced weight gain, reduced liver fat, increased fecal mass and higher concentration of short chain [[fatty acid]]s and bile salt.<ref name="Cholesterol reducing and bile-acid binding properties of taioba (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) leaf in rats fed a high-fat diet" /> It has also shown a probiotic effect.<ref name="Aroids as underexplored tubers with potential health benefits">{{cite book |author1=Jehannara Calle |title=Advances in Food and Nutrition Research |author2=Nicola Gasparre |author3=Yaiza Benavent-Gil |author4=Cristina M. Rosell |date=2021 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-12-824580-4 |volume=97 |pages=319–359 |language=en-US |chapter=Chapter Eight – Aroids as underexplored tubers with potential health benefits |doi=10.1016/bs.afnr.2021.02.018 |pmid=34311903 |s2cid=234955983}}</ref> Another study has shown that tannia can stop the cell cycle and force [[apoptosis]] in a cancer cell.<ref name="Agronomic characteristics (varieties or landraces) and potential of Xanthosoma sagittifolium as food and starch source" /> Tannia also has been traditionally used to treat osteoporosis because of the high content of free calcium analyses. Studies have shown that the usage of tannia indeed is a feasible option for treatment for poorer communities without access to proper medication.<ref name="Xanthosoma sagittifolium and Laportea aestuans: Species used to prevent osteoporosis in Brazilian traditional medicine">{{Cite journal |last1=de Oliveira |first1=Gisele Lopes |last2=Holanda Cavalcanti Andrade |first2=Laise de |last3=Morais de Oliveira |first3=Antonio Fernando |date=2012 |title=''Xanthosoma sagittifolium'' and ''Laportea aestuans'': Species used to prevent osteoporosis in Brazilian traditional medicine |journal=Pharmaceutical Biology |language=en |volume=50 |issue=7 |pages=930–932 |doi=10.3109/13880209.2011.637054 |issn=1388-0209 |pmid=22468879 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Cocoa trees can grow in direct sunlight, but in some climates, the intense light in the afternoon can damage the leaves.
Tannia has many leaves which makes it a good candidate for a [[cover crop]] that can protect the cocoa plant from direct sunlight.  Another advantage of Tannia is that it can grow in many different climates and therefore would be suitable for many different countries.<ref name="Utilizing cocoyam (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) for food and nutrition security: A review" />

Tannia could also be used to make food preservatives ([[lactic acid]]),<ref name="Agronomic characteristics (varieties or landraces) and potential of Xanthosoma sagittifolium as food and starch source" /> energy bars,<ref name="Aroids as underexplored tubers with potential health benefits" /> chips and crisps, additives in beverages, sauce thickeners, purees, and sauces.<ref name="Utilizing cocoyam (Xanthosoma sagittifolium) for food and nutrition security: A review" />
 
There is also a possibility of using tannia to make ethanol for [[biofuel]] because of the high starch content and the high yield.<ref name="Agronomic characteristics (varieties or landraces) and potential of Xanthosoma sagittifolium as food and starch source" />
